## Original idea
{
  "title": "Disentangling Competing Calibration Biases via Geometry-Aware Activation Steering",
  "core_problem": "LLM miscalibration arises from at least two competing biases — choice-supportive bias (inflating confidence in initial answers) and contradictory-evidence overweighting (causing excessive confidence revision under criticism) — that require opposing corrections. Existing calibration methods apply uniform corrections that cannot simultaneously address biases pulling confidence in opposite directions. Recent work (Liu, 2605.05715) further reveals a classification-correction gap: failure-mode directions that are linearly decodable may not be linearly steerable due to entanglement with task-critical computation (specificity ratio ≤0.152). This means even if competing biases can be identified in activations, correcting them requires knowing not just WHICH bias dominates but WHETHER each bias direction is steerable — and routing to appropriate interventions (linear rotation, non-linear correction, or selective abstention) accordingly. Can we jointly diagnose per-instance bias dominance AND steerability to apply targeted, manifold-preserving corrections where possible and graceful degradation where not?",
  "opportunity": "Kumaran et al. (Nature Machine Intelligence, 2026; arXiv 2507.03120) identified that LLM miscalibration results from two mechanistically distinct behavioral biases in Gemma 3, GPT-4o, and o1-preview: choice-supportive bias inflates confidence in selected answers, while contradictory-advice overweighting causes models to over-react to opposing evidence. Miao & Ungar (arXiv 2603.25052, 2026) independently showed that calibration and verbalized confidence signals are encoded linearly but orthogonally in the residual stream across three 7-8B models, establishing that confidence-related constructs have accessible geometric structure. Liu (arXiv 2605.05715, May 2026) demonstrated a critical classification-correction gap: linearly decodable failure directions (71.6% balanced accuracy) yield Δ≈0 under 29 steering configurations because the failure directions have 85-88% overlap with task-critical computation (specificity ratio ≤0.152) — but crucially, the paper also shows that (a) a learned non-linear residual MLP achieves Δ=+2.8pp where all linear methods fail, and (b) the decodable signal still supports selective abstention (AUROC 0.610, outperforming 5 uncertainty baselines). The 'Confidence Manifold' study (arXiv 2602.08159) found correctness signals occupy only 3-8 dimensions with simple mean-shift geometry across 9 models, suggesting that for calibration-related directions, the geometric structure may be more favorable than for the medical overthinking phenomenon Liu studied. The convergence of (a) identified competing biases, (b) linear confidence encoding evidence, (c) the decodable-steerable distinction with quantitative diagnostics, and (d) both norm-preserving rotation (Spherical Steering, ICML 2026) and collateral-damage-aware optimization (COAST, 2605.01167) creates an opportunity for a principled pipeline: diagnose bias identity, assess steerability, and route to the appropriate intervention.",
  "landscape": "Kumaran et al. (Nature MI, 2026) identified competing biases (CSB and CEO) via behavioral experiments on Gemma 3, GPT-4o, and o1-preview but proposed no correction framework and provided no mechanistic (activation-level) evidence. Miao & Ungar (arXiv 2603.25052, 2026) demonstrated that calibration accuracy and verbalized confidence are linearly encoded but orthogonal in 7-8B models (cosine similarity <0.04 across layers), and introduced adaptive steering achieving 4-7× ECE improvement — but they target the confidence-accuracy misalignment gap, not the competing bias structure. Tsujimura & Tagade (arXiv 2508.17182, Aug 2025) decomposed LLM assertiveness into emotional and logical sub-components via unsupervised clustering on Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct (645 samples), finding two clusters in high-assertive representations — methodologically adjacent but critically different: their decomposition is descriptive (post-hoc ChatGPT-labeled clusters of communication style) rather than causally grounded in identified cognitive biases, uses a single 1B model, reports no calibration metrics, and addresses assertiveness rather than calibration. The 'Wired for Overconfidence' paper (2604.01457, April 2026) identifies overconfidence circuits in Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.2-3B, achieving 96.9% ECE reduction on PopQA via monolithic activation steering, but only tests 3B models and treats overconfidence as a single phenomenon. Liu (arXiv 2605.05715, May 2026) is the most directly relevant recent advance: the paper demonstrates a classification-correction gap where linearly decodable failure directions (71.6% balanced accuracy on Llama-3.1-8B) yield Δ≈0 across five families of linear steering (29 configurations) because the failure direction has 85-88% overlap with task-critical computation (specificity ratio ≤0.152). Three convergent evidence lines confirm entanglement: low specificity, shared-direction steering damages accuracy (-12.1pp), and LEACE concept erasure damages accuracy (-3.6pp). Crucially, a learned non-linear bottleneck MLP (4096→64→4096) achieves Δ=+2.8pp (p=0.025) where linear methods fail, though with 8.2% damage rate — demonstrating that partial disentanglement is possible via non-linear transforms. The paper proposes the specificity ratio as a pre-intervention diagnostic and recommends selective abstention (AUROC 0.610) when steering fails. However, this was studied for medical overthinking, a single failure mode; whether calibration biases (CSB/CEO) exhibit similar or different entanglement profiles is an open question. Ji et al. (EMNLP 2025) modulates a single Verbal Uncertainty Feature direction, reducing hallucinations by ~30%, capturing only the net effect of competing biases. Joshi et al. (EMNLP 2025) found a single calibration direction but did not decompose it. CORAL (arXiv 2602.06022, Feb 2026) achieves 49% ECE improvement via correctness-subspace probing on 7B models but uses a single MLP probe direction. The 'Confidence Manifold' study (arXiv 2602.08159, Feb 2026) found correctness signals occupy 3-8 dimensions with simple mean-shift geometry across 9 models from 5 families, and causally validated via steering (10.9pp error rate change) — importantly, the low dimensionality and linear separability of correctness signals contrasts with Liu's high-entanglement finding for overthinking, suggesting calibration-related directions may have more favorable specificity profiles. Wang & Stengel-Eskin (ICLR 2026) introduced DINCO to normalize suggestibility bias via self-generated distractors at the output level. Zhuang et al. (arXiv 2025) proposed RDG to alleviate choice-supportive bias through fine-tuning but did not address CEO. CCPS (arXiv 2025) achieves ~55% ECE reduction via representation stability probing on MMLU. 'Breaking the Mirror' (arXiv 2509.03647) found that self-preference bias 'spans multiple or nonlinear directions,' achieving 97% unjustified bias reduction but with instability on legitimate cases — a direct warning that some biases may not be linearly separable. On the steering methodology side, the landscape has rapidly matured: Spherical Steering (arXiv 2602.08169, ICML 2026) performs norm-preserving geodesic rotation, outperforming addition-based baselines by +10% on TruthfulQA while maintaining generation quality. Selective Steering (Dang & Ngo, arXiv 2601.19375, Jan 2026) independently developed norm-preserving rotation with discriminative layer selection — applying steering only where feature representations exhibit opposite-signed class alignment, achieving 5.5× higher attack success rates with zero perplexity violations across 8 models from 3 families (Llama, Qwen, Gemma). COAST (Nguyen et al., arXiv 2605.01167, May 2026) formalizes collateral damage from steering interventions as unintended alignment changes along non-target feature directions, models steering as a constrained optimization minimizing expected squared collateral change weighted by the empirical second-moment matrix of activations, achieving up to 30% improvement over Angular Steering with strong negative correlation (r<-0.9) between collateral damage and accuracy loss across six benchmarks. AUSteer (arXiv 2602.04428, Feb 2026) decomposes block activations into fine-grained atomic units, steering fewer activations more precisely. CLAS (arXiv 2604.24693, Apr 2026) dynamically adapts steering strengths per-context across 11 benchmarks and 4 model families. 'Steered LLM Activations are Non-Surjective' (2604.09839, April 2026) formally proved that additive steering pushes activations off-manifold; 'A Sober Look at Steering Vectors' (NeurIPS 2024) showed many behaviors are unsteerable. No existing method jointly diagnoses which calibration bias dominates, assesses the steerability of each bias direction (via specificity ratio or equivalent), and routes to bias-specific interventions that range from manifold-preserving rotation to learned non-linear correction to selective abstention — yet the competing effects of CSB and CEO on calibration, combined with the now-established decodable-steerable gap, mean that both uniform correction AND uniform intervention strategy are fundamentally suboptimal.",
  "inspired_by": "Gap: Competing biases create non-uniform miscalibration patterns that single-direction methods cannot fix (Kumaran et al. 2026), while the classification-correction gap (Liu, 2605.05715) shows that decodable directions are not necessarily steerable — meaning Phase 1's separability validation is necessary but insufficient. Pattern: Theory-driven contrastive probing (Miao & Ungar 2026) + steerability diagnostics (specificity ratio, Liu 2026) + adaptive intervention routing (geometry-aware rotation for steerable directions, learned non-linear correction for entangled directions). Untried combination: Cognitive-bias-grounded contrastive stimuli → per-instance bias diagnosis → specificity-informed intervention routing (Spherical Steering / non-linear MLP / selective abstention), with the hypothesis that CSB and CEO may have asymmetric steerability profiles — which would explain why monolithic steering sometimes succeeds and sometimes fails at calibration correction.",
  "approach": "We design DBS-v2 (Disentangled Bias Steering) in three phases, now incorporating the critical distinction between decodability and steerability identified by Liu (2605.05715).\n\n**Phase 1 — Assumption Validation & Steerability Assessment (Weeks 1-5):** This phase tests TWO assumptions, not one: (A) that CSB and CEO produce distinguishable activation signatures, and (B) that identified directions are steerable without catastrophic collateral damage.\n\n*Phase 1A — Separability (Weeks 1-3):* We construct two contrastive stimulus sets: for CSB, we compare hidden states when the model reviews its own prior answer vs. a fresh unattributed answer (eliciting choice-supportive inflation); for CEO, we compare states when contradictory expert advice is present vs. absent (eliciting evidence overweighting). Using difference-in-means on these contrastive pairs, we extract candidate bias directions in the residual stream. We validate separability via: (a) cosine similarity between candidate directions, (b) principal angle analysis between CSB and CEO subspaces using the methodology of Miao & Ungar (2026), (c) PCA to assess whether 2 directions capture sufficient variance vs. requiring higher-dimensional subspaces, (d) ICA to test whether statistically independent (not just orthogonal) components emerge, and (e) cross-prediction ablations to confirm removing one bias subspace does not collapse the other. If CSB and CEO directions show cosine similarity >0.3 or shared variance >15%, we activate the separability fallback: extracting a multi-direction bias subspace via SAE-derived features and training a subspace projection classifier.\n\n*Phase 1B — Steerability Diagnostics (Weeks 3-5):* This is a critical addition motivated by Liu (2605.05715). Even if CSB and CEO are separable (Phase 1A succeeds), steering along identified directions may fail if those directions are entangled with task-critical computation. For each identified bias direction, we compute: (a) the **specificity ratio** — the proportion of mode-specific variance vs. shared variance with the correct-vs-incorrect subspace, following Liu's shared-specific decomposition methodology. Concretely, we extract the correctness subspace (correct vs. incorrect answer centroids), then decompose each bias direction into a component within this subspace (shared) and a component orthogonal to it (mode-specific). The specificity ratio = ||mode-specific||² / ||total||². (b) **Within-class variance analysis** — comparing within-class variance to inter-centroid gap for each bias direction (Liu's second diagnostic). (c) **LEACE concept erasure test** — applying concept erasure to each bias direction and measuring accuracy damage as causal evidence of entanglement. (d) **Cross-architecture stability** — verifying specificity ratios are consistent across model families.\n\nWe establish quantitative thresholds informed by Liu's findings: specificity ratio ≥0.5 → HIGH steerability (linear rotation expected to work); 0.2-0.5 → MEDIUM (rotation may partially work, monitor collateral damage); <0.2 → LOW (linear steering unlikely to succeed, route to non-linear intervention). These thresholds are calibrated against Liu's findings where specificity ≤0.152 yielded Δ≈0 for linear steering while ≥0.999 succeeded for refusal steering. Crucially, we hypothesize that CSB and CEO may have ASYMMETRIC specificity profiles — one may be more steerable than the other — which would provide a mechanistic explanation for why monolithic calibration steering sometimes succeeds partially.\n\nPhase 1 results constitute an independent contribution: the first joint separability-and-steerability assessment of behaviorally-identified competing biases, providing the field's first specificity ratio measurements for calibration-related bias directions.\n\n**Phase 2 — Per-Instance Bias Diagnosis (Weeks 4-8):** A lightweight logistic probe (or, in the fallback case, a small MLP) trained on per-instance projection magnitudes onto each bias direction classifies which bias dominates for a given query. We stratify by difficulty: on easy questions where models are already confident, CSB likely dominates; on hard questions under criticism, CEO likely dominates. The probe output provides a continuous dominance score. NEW: The Phase 1B steerability assessment informs a per-direction intervention routing table, so the probe's output determines not only which bias is active but which intervention to apply.\n\n**Phase 3 — Adaptive Geometry-Aware Intervention (Weeks 6-14):** Instead of a single intervention strategy, Phase 3 now implements an adaptive routing pipeline informed by Phase 1B's steerability diagnostics:\n\n*Route A — Spherical Steering (for HIGH-specificity directions):* When a bias direction has specificity ratio ≥0.5, we adopt Spherical Steering (You et al., ICML 2026) as the primary intervention: rotating activations along a geodesic away from the dominant bias direction while preserving activation norms. This addresses the off-manifold concern (Mishra et al., 2604.09839) while the high specificity ensures minimal collateral damage to task-critical computation. A confidence gate modulates rotation magnitude based on the probe's dominance score. We note that Selective Steering (Dang & Ngo, 2601.19375) provides an alternative norm-preserving formulation with discriminative layer selection; we ablate both to determine which is more effective for calibration-specific interventions.\n\n*Route B — Learned Non-Linear Residual Correction (for LOW-specificity directions):* When a bias direction has specificity ratio <0.2, linear steering of any kind (additive, rotational, or projected) is expected to fail due to entanglement with task-critical computation (Liu, 2605.05715). Following Liu's finding that a bottleneck residual MLP (d→64→d) achieves Δ=+2.8pp where all 29 linear configurations yield Δ≈0, we train a small non-linear residual adapter per bias type. The adapter takes the hidden state as input and outputs a residual correction, trained via supervision on (biased state, corrected state) pairs extracted from the contrastive dataset. We incorporate the COAST framework (Nguyen et al., 2605.01167) by weighting the training loss by the empirical second-moment matrix to minimize expected collateral damage along non-target feature directions. The adapter's bottleneck architecture (d→64→d, <0.1% of model parameters) keeps the intervention lightweight and inference-efficient.\n\n*Route C — Selective Abstention (for UNSTEERABLE directions):* When Phase 1B indicates low specificity AND Phase 3 ablations confirm that neither Route A nor Route B improves calibration without excessive damage (>5% accuracy degradation), we leverage the decodable signal for selective abstention: the bias probe flags instances where the dominant bias has high activation but low steerability, outputting a reliability score. Following Liu's demonstration that decodable signals support post-generation reliability estimation (AUROC 0.610) even when correction fails, this provides a graceful degradation path.\n\n*Route D — Medium-Specificity Hybrid (for intermediate cases):* For directions with specificity 0.2-0.5, we apply Spherical Steering with conservative rotation magnitude (capped at 50% of the high-specificity coefficient) and monitor collateral damage via the COAST second-moment diagnostic. If per-instance collateral damage exceeds a threshold, we fall back to Route B for that instance.\n\nWe evaluate on TriviaQA, MMLU, PopQA, and NQ-Open across Gemma 4 31B (Dense), Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. We additionally include Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.2-3B as supplementary models to enable fair comparison with 'Wired for Overconfidence' results at the same scale. Metrics: ECE, Brier score, AUROC, difficulty-stratified ECE (easy/medium/hard partitions), AND NEW: per-direction specificity ratios, collateral damage measurements (accuracy on non-target tasks before/after steering), and route-distribution analysis (what fraction of instances are routed to each intervention). Baselines: temperature scaling, CCPS, VUF intervention, DINCO, CORAL, Miao & Ungar adaptive steering, monolithic circuit ablation (Wired for Overconfidence replication at 3B scale), monolithic Spherical Steering (single direction, no bias decomposition), and NEW: monolithic non-linear residual MLP (single direction, no bias decomposition) to isolate the contribution of bias decomposition from the contribution of non-linear correction.",

  "description": "We propose DBS-v2 (Disentangled Bias Steering), a method that separately identifies, assesses the steerability of, and adaptively corrects two competing sources of LLM miscalibration identified by Kumaran et al. (2026): choice-supportive bias (CSB, inflating confidence in selected answers) and contradictory-evidence overweighting (CEO, causing excessive confidence revision under criticism). Unlike Tsujimura & Tagade (2025), who descriptively decomposed assertiveness into emotion/logic clusters via unsupervised methods on a 1B model without calibration evaluation, DBS-v2 is grounded in causally-identified cognitive biases with theory-driven contrastive stimuli and directly targets calibration metrics.\n\nA critical insight motivating this revision is the classification-correction gap demonstrated by Liu (2605.05715): linearly decodable failure directions (71.6% balanced accuracy) can yield Δ≈0 under steering because they overlap 85-88% with task-critical computation. This means that separability (Phase 1A) is necessary but insufficient — we must also assess steerability before committing to an intervention strategy.\n\nThe method proceeds in three phases. Phase 1A (Separability Validation) tests whether CSB and CEO produce distinguishable activation signatures using contrastive activation probing, validated via cosine similarity, principal angle analysis, PCA/ICA dimensionality assessment, and cross-prediction ablation (following Miao & Ungar, 2026). Phase 1B (Steerability Assessment) — the key new addition — computes the specificity ratio (mode-specific vs. shared variance with the correct/incorrect subspace) for each identified bias direction, following Liu's shared-specific decomposition methodology. This diagnostic distinguishes between directions that are decodable-and-steerable vs. decodable-but-entangled. We hypothesize that CSB and CEO may have asymmetric specificity profiles, which would explain why monolithic calibration steering yields inconsistent results across settings. The Confidence Manifold study (2602.08159) provides encouraging evidence that correctness-related signals occupy only 3-8 dimensions with simple mean-shift geometry, suggesting calibration-related directions may have more favorable specificity than the medical overthinking phenomenon Liu studied.\n\nPhase 2 trains a lightweight per-instance bias dominance classifier whose output determines both which bias is active and which intervention route to apply. Phase 3 implements adaptive routing: (Route A) Spherical Steering for high-specificity directions (≥0.5), with Selective Steering (Dang & Ngo, 2601.19375) as an ablation alternative providing discriminative layer selection; (Route B) a learned non-linear bottleneck residual MLP (d→64→d) for low-specificity directions (<0.2), trained with COAST-informed (Nguyen et al., 2605.01167) collateral-damage-aware loss weighting; (Route C) selective abstention leveraging the decodable signal for reliability estimation when neither linear nor non-linear correction is safe; and (Route D) conservative hybrid steering for intermediate specificity (0.2-0.5).\n\nWe evaluate on TriviaQA, MMLU, PopQA, and NQ-Open across five models: Gemma 4 31B (Dense), Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as primary targets, plus Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.2-3B for fair comparison with 'Wired for Overconfidence' baselines. We compare against temperature scaling, CCPS, VUF intervention, DINCO, CORAL, Miao & Ungar adaptive steering, monolithic Spherical Steering (without bias decomposition), and monolithic non-linear MLP (without bias decomposition). The primary contributions are: (1) the first joint separability-and-steerability assessment of competing calibration biases, providing specificity ratio measurements that the field currently lacks; (2) interpretable, bias-specific diagnostics revealing which bias source drives miscalibration per-instance AND whether it is correctable; (3) adaptive intervention routing that gracefully degrades from manifold-preserving rotation to non-linear correction to selective abstention based on measured entanglement; and (4) the hypothesis that CSB and CEO have asymmetric steerability profiles, offering a mechanistic explanation for inconsistent monolithic steering results. Phase 1 results constitute an independent contribution regardless of Phase 2-3 outcomes.",

We differentiate from Liu by (a) studying calibration biases rather than medical overthinking, (b) testing multiple competing directions rather than a single failure mode, (c) hypothesizing asymmetric steerability profiles, and (d) providing the Confidence Manifold evidence (2602.08159) that calibration-related directions may have more favorable geometry.",

Route C (selective abstention) added as ultimate fallback. Route D (conservative hybrid) added for intermediate specificity. ## Reviewer feedback (round 3)
Issues: ["MISSING CRITICAL BASELINE: MERA ('To Steer or Not to Steer?', Hedström et al., ICML 2025, arXiv 2510.13290) implements selective steering with adaptive strength and abstention — directly overlapping with Routes C and D. MERA optimizes intervention direction AND calibrates when/how much to steer, with provable non-degradation guarantees. It can be applied ON TOP of existing steering methods. This must be cited as a baseline and distinguished from: DBS-v2 decomposes biases while MERA treats errors monolithically; DBS-v2 routes between intervention types while MERA modulates a single intervention's strength.", "MISSING NONLINEAR STEERING COMPETITORS: The landscape fails to cite (a) Curveball Steering (arXiv 2603.09313, March 2026) — polynomial kernel PCA-based nonlinear steering that explicitly addresses geometric distortion in activation spaces, directly relevant to the linear vs. nonlinear routing rationale; (b) FLAS (arXiv 2605.05892, May 2026) — flow-based activation steering learning concept-conditioned velocity fields, first method to outperform prompting on AxBench; (c) ODESteer (arXiv 2602.17560, ICLR 2026) — ODE-based multi-step adaptive steering with barrier functions. These represent the rapidly maturing nonlinear steering landscape that Route B must be positioned against.", "AAAI 2027 PRIMARY TARGET IS INFEASIBLE: The full paper deadline is July 28, 2026 — approximately 10 weeks from now. The manual timeline estimate is 16-20 weeks. Even the auto_research timeline (6-10 weeks) is at the edge, and auto_research is the most expensive mode. {
  "title": "Disentangling Competing Calibration Biases via Geometry-Aware Activation Steering",
  "core_problem": "LLM miscalibration arises from at least two competing biases — choice-supportive bias (inflating confidence in initial answers) and contradictory-evidence overweighting (causing excessive confidence revision under criticism) — that require opposing corrections. Existing calibration methods apply uniform corrections that cannot simultaneously address biases pulling confidence in opposite directions. Recent work (Liu, 2605.05715) further reveals a classification-correction gap: failure-mode directions that are linearly decodable may not be linearly steerable due to entanglement with task-critical computation (specificity ratio ≤0.152). This means even if competing biases can be identified in activations, correcting them requires knowing not just WHICH bias dominates but WHETHER each bias direction is steerable — and routing to appropriate interventions (linear rotation, non-linear correction, or selective abstention) accordingly. Can we jointly diagnose per-instance bias dominance AND steerability to apply targeted, manifold-preserving corrections where possible and graceful degradation where not?",
  "opportunity": "Kumaran et al. (Nature Machine Intelligence, 2026; arXiv 2507.03120) identified that LLM miscalibration results from two mechanistically distinct behavioral biases in Gemma 3, GPT-4o, and o1-preview: choice-supportive bias inflates confidence in selected answers, while contradictory-advice overweighting causes models to over-react to opposing evidence. Miao & Ungar (arXiv 2603.25052, 2026) independently showed that calibration and verbalized confidence signals are encoded linearly but orthogonally in the residual stream across three 7-8B models, establishing that confidence-related constructs have accessible geometric structure. Liu (arXiv 2605.05715, May 2026) demonstrated a critical classification-correction gap: linearly decodable failure directions (71.6% balanced accuracy) yield Δ≈0 under 29 steering configurations because the failure directions have 85-88% overlap with task-critical computation (specificity ratio ≤0.152) — but crucially, the paper also shows that (a) a learned non-linear residual MLP achieves Δ=+2.8pp where all linear methods fail, and (b) the decodable signal still supports selective abstention (AUROC 0.610, outperforming 5 uncertainty baselines). The 'Confidence Manifold' study (arXiv 2602.08159) found correctness signals occupy only 3-8 dimensions with simple mean-shift geometry across 9 models, suggesting that for calibration-related directions, the geometric structure may be more favorable than for the medical overthinking phenomenon Liu studied. The convergence of (a) identified competing biases, (b) linear confidence encoding evidence, (c) the decodable-steerable distinction with quantitative diagnostics, and (d) both norm-preserving rotation (Spherical Steering, ICML 2026) and collateral-damage-aware optimization (COAST, 2605.01167) creates an opportunity for a principled pipeline: diagnose bias identity, assess steerability, and route to the appropriate intervention.",
  "landscape": "Kumaran et al. (Nature MI, 2026) identified competing biases (CSB and CEO) via behavioral experiments on Gemma 3, GPT-4o, and o1-preview but proposed no correction framework and provided no mechanistic (activation-level) evidence. Miao & Ungar (arXiv 2603.25052, 2026) demonstrated that calibration accuracy and verbalized confidence are linearly encoded but orthogonal in 7-8B models (cosine similarity <0.04 across layers), and introduced adaptive steering achieving 4-7× ECE improvement — but they target the confidence-accuracy misalignment gap, not the competing bias structure. Tsujimura & Tagade (arXiv 2508.17182, Aug 2025) decomposed LLM assertiveness into emotional and logical sub-components via unsupervised clustering on Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct (645 samples), finding two clusters in high-assertive representations — methodologically adjacent but critically different: their decomposition is descriptive (post-hoc ChatGPT-labeled clusters of communication style) rather than causally grounded in identified cognitive biases, uses a single 1B model, reports no calibration metrics, and addresses assertiveness rather than calibration. The 'Wired for Overconfidence' paper (2604.01457, April 2026) identifies overconfidence circuits in Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.2-3B, achieving 96.9% ECE reduction on PopQA via monolithic activation steering, but only tests 3B models and treats overconfidence as a single phenomenon. Liu (arXiv 2605.05715, May 2026) is the most directly relevant recent advance: the paper demonstrates a classification-correction gap where linearly decodable failure directions (71.6% balanced accuracy on Llama-3.1-8B) yield Δ≈0 across five families of linear steering (29 configurations) because the failure direction has 85-88% overlap with task-critical computation (specificity ratio ≤0.152). Three convergent evidence lines confirm entanglement: low specificity, shared-direction steering damages accuracy (-12.1pp), and LEACE concept erasure damages accuracy (-3.6pp). Crucially, a learned non-linear bottleneck MLP (4096→64→4096) achieves Δ=+2.8pp (p=0.025) where linear methods fail, though with 8.2% damage rate — demonstrating that partial disentanglement is possible via non-linear transforms. The paper proposes the specificity ratio as a pre-intervention diagnostic and recommends selective abstention (AUROC 0.610) when steering fails. However, this was studied for medical overthinking, a single failure mode; whether calibration biases (CSB/CEO) exhibit similar or different entanglement profiles is an open question. Ji et al. (EMNLP 2025) modulates a single Verbal Uncertainty Feature direction, reducing hallucinations by ~30%, capturing only the net effect of competing biases. Joshi et al. (EMNLP 2025) found a single calibration direction but did not decompose it. CORAL (arXiv 2602.06022, Feb 2026) achieves 49% ECE improvement via correctness-subspace probing on 7B models but uses a single MLP probe direction. The 'Confidence Manifold' study (arXiv 2602.08159, Feb 2026) found correctness signals occupy 3-8 dimensions with simple mean-shift geometry across 9 models from 5 families, and causally validated via steering (10.9pp error rate change) — importantly, the low dimensionality and linear separability of correctness signals contrasts with Liu's high-entanglement finding for overthinking, suggesting calibration-related directions may have more favorable specificity profiles. Wang & Stengel-Eskin (ICLR 2026) introduced DINCO to normalize suggestibility bias via self-generated distractors at the output level. Zhuang et al. (arXiv 2025) proposed RDG to alleviate choice-supportive bias through fine-tuning but did not address CEO. CCPS (arXiv 2025) achieves ~55% ECE reduction via representation stability probing on MMLU. 'Breaking the Mirror' (arXiv 2509.03647) found that self-preference bias 'spans multiple or nonlinear directions,' achieving 97% unjustified bias reduction but with instability on legitimate cases — a direct warning that some biases may not be linearly separable. On the steering methodology side, the landscape has rapidly matured: Spherical Steering (arXiv 2602.08169, ICML 2026) performs norm-preserving geodesic rotation, outperforming addition-based baselines by +10% on TruthfulQA while maintaining generation quality. Selective Steering (Dang & Ngo, arXiv 2601.19375, Jan 2026) independently developed norm-preserving rotation with discriminative layer selection — applying steering only where feature representations exhibit opposite-signed class alignment, achieving 5.5× higher attack success rates with zero perplexity violations across 8 models from 3 families (Llama, Qwen, Gemma). COAST (Nguyen et al., arXiv 2605.01167, May 2026) formalizes collateral damage from steering interventions as unintended alignment changes along non-target feature directions, models steering as a constrained optimization minimizing expected squared collateral change weighted by the empirical second-moment matrix of activations, achieving up to 30% improvement over Angular Steering with strong negative correlation (r<-0.9) between collateral damage and accuracy loss across six benchmarks. AUSteer (arXiv 2602.04428, Feb 2026) decomposes block activations into fine-grained atomic units, steering fewer activations more precisely. CLAS (arXiv 2604.24693, Apr 2026) dynamically adapts steering strengths per-context across 11 benchmarks and 4 model families. 'Steered LLM Activations are Non-Surjective' (2604.09839, April 2026) formally proved that additive steering pushes activations off-manifold; 'A Sober Look at Steering Vectors' (NeurIPS 2024) showed many behaviors are unsteerable. No existing method jointly diagnoses which calibration bias dominates, assesses the steerability of each bias direction (via specificity ratio or equivalent), and routes to bias-specific interventions that range from manifold-preserving rotation to learned non-linear correction to selective abstention — yet the competing effects of CSB and CEO on calibration, combined with the now-established decodable-steerable gap, mean that both uniform correction AND uniform intervention strategy are fundamentally suboptimal.",
  "inspired_by": "Gap: Competing biases create non-uniform miscalibration patterns that single-direction methods cannot fix (Kumaran et al. 2026), while the classification-correction gap (Liu, 2605.05715) shows that decodable directions are not necessarily steerable — meaning Phase 1's separability validation is necessary but insufficient. Pattern: Theory-driven contrastive probing (Miao & Ungar 2026) + steerability diagnostics (specificity ratio, Liu 2026) + adaptive intervention routing (geometry-aware rotation for steerable directions, learned non-linear correction for entangled directions). Untried combination: Cognitive-bias-grounded contrastive stimuli → per-instance bias diagnosis → specificity-informed intervention routing (Spherical Steering / non-linear MLP / selective abstention), with the hypothesis that CSB and CEO may have asymmetric steerability profiles — which would explain why monolithic steering sometimes succeeds and sometimes fails at calibration correction.",
  "approach": "We design DBS-v2 (Disentangled Bias Steering) in three phases, now incorporating the critical distinction between decodability and steerability identified by Liu (2605.05715).\n\n**Phase 1 — Assumption Validation & Steerability Assessment (Weeks 1-5):** This phase tests TWO assumptions, not one: (A) that CSB and CEO produce distinguishable activation signatures, and (B) that identified directions are steerable without catastrophic collateral damage.\n\n*Phase 1A — Separability (Weeks 1-3):* We construct two contrastive stimulus sets: for CSB, we compare hidden states when the model reviews its own prior answer vs. a fresh unattributed answer (eliciting choice-supportive inflation); for CEO, we compare states when contradictory expert advice is present vs. absent (eliciting evidence overweighting). Using difference-in-means on these contrastive pairs, we extract candidate bias directions in the residual stream. We validate separability via: (a) cosine similarity between candidate directions, (b) principal angle analysis between CSB and CEO subspaces using the methodology of Miao & Ungar (2026), (c) PCA to assess whether 2 directions capture sufficient variance vs. requiring higher-dimensional subspaces, (d) ICA to test whether statistically independent (not just orthogonal) components emerge, and (e) cross-prediction ablations to confirm removing one bias subspace does not collapse the other. If CSB and CEO directions show cosine similarity >0.3 or shared variance >15%, we activate the separability fallback: extracting a multi-direction bias subspace via SAE-derived features and training a subspace projection classifier.\n\n*Phase 1B — Steerability Diagnostics (Weeks 3-5):* This is a critical addition motivated by Liu (2605.05715). Even if CSB and CEO are separable (Phase 1A succeeds), steering along identified directions may fail if those directions are entangled with task-critical computation. For each identified bias direction, we compute: (a) the **specificity ratio** — the proportion of mode-specific variance vs. shared variance with the correct-vs-incorrect subspace, following Liu's shared-specific decomposition methodology. Concretely, we extract the correctness subspace (correct vs. incorrect answer centroids), then decompose each bias direction into a component within this subspace (shared) and a component orthogonal to it (mode-specific). The specificity ratio = ||mode-specific||² / ||total||². (b) **Within-class variance analysis** — comparing within-class variance to inter-centroid gap for each bias direction (Liu's second diagnostic). (c) **LEACE concept erasure test** — applying concept erasure to each bias direction and measuring accuracy damage as causal evidence of entanglement. (d) **Cross-architecture stability** — verifying specificity ratios are consistent across model families.\n\nWe establish quantitative thresholds informed by Liu's findings: specificity ratio ≥0.5 → HIGH steerability (linear rotation expected to work); 0.2-0.5 → MEDIUM (rotation may partially work, monitor collateral damage); <0.2 → LOW (linear steering unlikely to succeed, route to non-linear intervention). These thresholds are calibrated against Liu's findings where specificity ≤0.152 yielded Δ≈0 for linear steering while ≥0.999 succeeded for refusal steering. Crucially, we hypothesize that CSB and CEO may have ASYMMETRIC specificity profiles — one may be more steerable than the other — which would provide a mechanistic explanation for why monolithic calibration steering sometimes succeeds partially.\n\nPhase 1 results constitute an independent contribution: the first joint separability-and-steerability assessment of behaviorally-identified competing biases, providing the field's first specificity ratio measurements for calibration-related bias directions.\n\n**Phase 2 — Per-Instance Bias Diagnosis (Weeks 4-8):** A lightweight logistic probe (or, in the fallback case, a small MLP) trained on per-instance projection magnitudes onto each bias direction classifies which bias dominates for a given query. We stratify by difficulty: on easy questions where models are already confident, CSB likely dominates; on hard questions under criticism, CEO likely dominates. The probe output provides a continuous dominance score. NEW: The Phase 1B steerability assessment informs a per-direction intervention routing table, so the probe's output determines not only which bias is active but which intervention to apply.\n\n**Phase 3 — Adaptive Geometry-Aware Intervention (Weeks 6-14):** Instead of a single intervention strategy, Phase 3 now implements an adaptive routing pipeline informed by Phase 1B's steerability diagnostics:\n\n*Route A — Spherical Steering (for HIGH-specificity directions):* When a bias direction has specificity ratio ≥0.5, we adopt Spherical Steering (You et al., ICML 2026) as the primary intervention: rotating activations along a geodesic away from the dominant bias direction while preserving activation norms. This addresses the off-manifold concern (Mishra et al., 2604.09839) while the high specificity ensures minimal collateral damage to task-critical computation. A confidence gate modulates rotation magnitude based on the probe's dominance score. We note that Selective Steering (Dang & Ngo, 2601.19375) provides an alternative norm-preserving formulation with discriminative layer selection; we ablate both to determine which is more effective for calibration-specific interventions.\n\n*Route B — Learned Non-Linear Residual Correction (for LOW-specificity directions):* When a bias direction has specificity ratio <0.2, linear steering of any kind (additive, rotational, or projected) is expected to fail due to entanglement with task-critical computation (Liu, 2605.05715). Following Liu's finding that a bottleneck residual MLP (d→64→d) achieves Δ=+2.8pp where all 29 linear configurations yield Δ≈0, we train a small non-linear residual adapter per bias type. The adapter takes the hidden state as input and outputs a residual correction, trained via supervision on (biased state, corrected state) pairs extracted from the contrastive dataset. We incorporate the COAST framework (Nguyen et al., 2605.01167) by weighting the training loss by the empirical second-moment matrix to minimize expected collateral damage along non-target feature directions. The adapter's bottleneck architecture (d→64→d, <0.1% of model parameters) keeps the intervention lightweight and inference-efficient.\n\n*Route C — Selective Abstention (for UNSTEERABLE directions):* When Phase 1B indicates low specificity AND Phase 3 ablations confirm that neither Route A nor Route B improves calibration without excessive damage (>5% accuracy degradation), we leverage the decodable signal for selective abstention: the bias probe flags instances where the dominant bias has high activation but low steerability, outputting a reliability score. Following Liu's demonstration that decodable signals support post-generation reliability estimation (AUROC 0.610) even when correction fails, this provides a graceful degradation path.\n\n*Route D — Medium-Specificity Hybrid (for intermediate cases):* For directions with specificity 0.2-0.5, we apply Spherical Steering with conservative rotation magnitude (capped at 50% of the high-specificity coefficient) and monitor collateral damage via the COAST second-moment diagnostic. If per-instance collateral damage exceeds a threshold, we fall back to Route B for that instance.\n\nWe evaluate on TriviaQA, MMLU, PopQA, and NQ-Open across Gemma 4 31B (Dense), Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. We additionally include Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.2-3B as supplementary models to enable fair comparison with 'Wired for Overconfidence' results at the same scale. Metrics: ECE, Brier score, AUROC, difficulty-stratified ECE (easy/medium/hard partitions), AND NEW: per-direction specificity ratios, collateral damage measurements (accuracy on non-target tasks before/after steering), and route-distribution analysis (what fraction of instances are routed to each intervention). Baselines: temperature scaling, CCPS, VUF intervention, DINCO, CORAL, Miao & Ungar adaptive steering, monolithic circuit ablation (Wired for Overconfidence replication at 3B scale), monolithic Spherical Steering (single direction, no bias decomposition), and NEW: monolithic non-linear residual MLP (single direction, no bias decomposition) to isolate the contribution of bias decomposition from the contribution of non-linear correction.",

  "description": "We propose DBS-v2 (Disentangled Bias Steering), a method that separately identifies, assesses the steerability of, and adaptively corrects two competing sources of LLM miscalibration identified by Kumaran et al. (2026): choice-supportive bias (CSB, inflating confidence in selected answers) and contradictory-evidence overweighting (CEO, causing excessive confidence revision under criticism). Unlike Tsujimura & Tagade (2025), who descriptively decomposed assertiveness into emotion/logic clusters via unsupervised methods on a 1B model without calibration evaluation, DBS-v2 is grounded in causally-identified cognitive biases with theory-driven contrastive stimuli and directly targets calibration metrics.\n\nA critical insight motivating this revision is the classification-correction gap demonstrated by Liu (2605.05715): linearly decodable failure directions (71.6% balanced accuracy) can yield Δ≈0 under steering because they overlap 85-88% with task-critical computation. The Confidence Manifold study (2602.08159) provides encouraging evidence that correctness-related signals occupy only 3-8 dimensions with simple mean-shift geometry, suggesting calibration-related directions may have more favorable specificity than the medical overthinking phenomenon Liu studied.\n\nPhase 2 trains a lightweight per-instance bias dominance classifier whose output determines both which bias is active and which intervention route to apply. Phase 3 implements adaptive routing: (Route A) Spherical Steering for high-specificity directions (≥0.5), with Selective Steering (Dang & Ngo, 2601.19375) as an ablation alternative providing discriminative layer selection; (Route B) a learned non-linear bottleneck residual MLP (d→64→d) for low-specificity directions (<0.2), trained with COAST-informed (Nguyen et al., 2605.01167) collateral-damage-aware loss weighting; (Route C) selective abstention leveraging the decodable signal for reliability estimation when neither linear nor non-linear correction is safe; and (Route D) conservative hybrid steering for intermediate specificity (0.2-0.5).\n\nWe evaluate on TriviaQA, MMLU, PopQA, and NQ-Open across five models: Gemma 4 31B (Dense), Qwen3-8B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct as primary targets, plus Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.2-3B for fair comparison with 'Wired for Overconfidence' baselines. Phase 1 results constitute an independent contribution regardless of Phase 2-3 outcomes.",

Based on the search results, here's what I found about this paper:

## Paper Overview

MERA (Mechanistic Error Reduction with Abstention) is a principled framework for steering language models to mitigate errors through selective, adaptive interventions. Unlike existing methods that rely on fixed, manually tuned steering strengths, MERA addresses these limitations by optimising the intervention direction and calibrating when and how much to steer, thereby provably improving performance or abstaining when no confident correction is possible.

## Key Features

Experiments across diverse datasets and LM families demonstrate safe, effective, non-degrading error correction and that MERA outperforms existing baselines. Moreover, MERA can be applied on top of existing steering techniques to further enhance their performance, establishing it as a general-purpose and efficient approach to mechanistic activation steering.

## Practical Approach

The method uses a lightweight helper model to first estimate how likely the language model is to be wrong, and then gently shifts the model's internal activity to reduce the probability of an error being made. If the input is already predicted to be correct, then MERA does nothing.

## Publication

The paper was published in the Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025). The arXiv preprint was submitted on October 15, 2025. The paper's code is also available on GitHub for the paper "To Steer or Not to Steer? Mechanistic Error Reduction with Abstention for Language Models" by Hedström et al.

I found the paper! Here's what I found about the research:

Curveball steering is a nonlinear steering method based on polynomial kernel PCA that performs interventions in a feature space, better respecting the learned activation geometry.

The paper addresses a key issue in activation steering for large language models. Existing methods largely rely on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, assuming behavioral attributes can be manipulated using global linear directions. However, the researchers observed substantial and concept-dependent distortions in activation spaces via measuring geometric distortion, indicating that activation spaces are not well-approximated by a globally linear geometry.

Curveball steering consistently outperforms linear PCA-based steering, particularly in regimes exhibiting strong geometric distortion, suggesting that geometry-aware, nonlinear steering provides a principled alternative to global, linear interventions.

The paper (arXiv 2603.09313) was authored by Shivam Raval, Hae Jin Song, Linlin Wu, Abir Harrasse, Jeff M. Phillips, Fazl Barez, and Amirali Abdullah, and was published in March 2026.

## FLAS (Flow-based Activation Steering)

FLAS learns a general, concept-conditioned velocity field that transports unsteered activations to steered ones without relying on simplifying assumptions. 

Activation steering has emerged as a promising alternative for controlling language-model behavior at inference time by modifying intermediate representations while keeping model parameters frozen. However, large-scale evaluations such as AxBench show that existing steering methods are often outperformed by simple in-context prompting and generalize poorly to unseen concepts.

The limitations of prior methods arise from unvalidated simplifying assumptions shared across prior methods, which typically restrict steering interventions to fixed, single-step, position-invariant transforms.

## Performance Results

On AxBench, FLAS is the first learned method to consistently outperform prompting, reaching held-out harmonic means of 1.015 on Gemma-2-2B-IT and 1.113 on Gemma-2-9B-IT.

The paper (arXiv:2605.05892) was posted on May 7, 2026, and represents a significant advancement in the activation steering field by introducing a more flexible approach based on flow-based methods rather than the linear transformations used in previous approaches.

## ODESteer: A Unified ODE-Based Steering Framework for LLM Alignment

ODESteer proposes a unified ordinary differential equations (ODEs)-based theoretical framework for activation steering in LLM alignment, where identifying a steering direction becomes equivalent to designing a barrier function from control theory.

### Key Innovation

ODESteer identifies steering directions by defining the barrier function as the log-density ratio between positive and negative activations, and employs it to construct an ODE for multi-step and adaptive steering. Conventional activation addition can be interpreted as a first-order approximation to the solution of an ODE.

### Problem Addressed

Current methods suffer from two key limitations: the lack of a unified theoretical framework for guiding the design of steering directions, and an over-reliance on one-step steering that fails to capture complex patterns of activation distributions.

### Results and Publication

The paper was published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026, and compared to state-of-the-art activation steering methods, ODESteer achieves consistent empirical improvements on diverse LLM alignment benchmarks.

# MERA Technical Details Extraction

## 1. Optimization of Intervention Direction

**Mathematical Formulation:**
MERA solves a constrained optimization problem:

```
min_v ||v||²₂  subject to  p̂(h+v) ≤ α
```

For linear probes where p̂(h) = w^T h, the closed-form solution is:

```
v* = {
  0,                              if w^T h ≤ α
  ((α - w^T h) / ||w||²₂) w,    if w^T h > α
}
```

This can be rewritten as v* = λ* w, where λ* = max(0, (α - w^T h) / ||w||²₂).

The steering vector is derived from linear error estimator probes trained to predict model error from activations, rather than from contrastive pairs.

## 2. Abstention Mechanism (When to Steer)

MERA uses threshold-based abstention via calibration:

- A steering threshold α* is selected on a separate calibration dataset
- "If no α yields a statistically significant improvement, we abstain from intervention"
- The valid threshold set is: αvalid = {α ∈ {α₁,...,αₖ} : Δcal(α) > ε + b(δ,K,N)}
- If αvalid is empty, λ* = 0 (no steering applied)

The method incorporates a confidence bound b(δ,K,N) = √(log(2K/δ)/(2N)) using Hoeffding inequality with Bonferroni correction.

## 3. Adaptive Strength Mechanism (How Much to Steer)

Steering strength scales proportionally with predicted error:

**Key property:** "The steering strength scales with the residual α - w^T h = α - p̂(h), leading to stronger adjustments for larger estimated errors."

The normalization by ||w||²₂ aligns with prior work on improving steering efficacy. This eliminates the need for manual hyperparameter sweeps of fixed scaling coefficients.

## 4. Provable Non-Degradation Guarantees

**Theoretical guarantee (Equation 9):**

```
ℙ(Δcal(α*) > ε) ≥ 1 - δ
```

"This ensures that, with probability at least 1−δ, the selected α* yields a genuine performance improvement that exceeds ε."

The guarantee applies assuming i.i.d. samples. It provides "either a provable improvement in performance or abstains from intervention if αvalid is empty."

Note: This guarantees improvement on the calibration set, not on unseen test data.

## 5. Experimental Setup

**Models:** LLaMA-3.2-1B, Gemma-2-2B, Qwen-2.5-3B (base and instruction-tuned variants)

**Datasets:** SMS Spam, Yes/No, Sentiment, MMLU-hs, MMLU-prof
- Label cardinalities: binary to quaternary
- Training samples: 2,600-300 with 30% validation split

**Probes:** Linear error estimators trained with sparsity constraints via L1 regularization

## 6. Key Quantitative Results

MERA improvements (Steering Performance Impact metric):

- **SMS Spam (LLaMA-1B):** +0.87 SPI
- **Yes/No (LLaMA-1B):** +0.52 SPI  
- **Sentiment (Gemma-2-2B):** +0.49 SPI
- **MMLU-hs (LLaMA-1B-IT):** +0.33 SPI

"Base models benefit more from MERA steering compared to instruction-tuned models."

Contrastive steering without MERA sometimes reduced accuracy (e.g., -0.05 SPI); with MERA calibration it improved to +0.52 SPI on Yes/No.

## 7. Composition with Other Methods

MERA functions as a general wrapper improving existing steering approaches:

- **MERA-μ₁₀₀:** Applies MERA's optimization and calibration to contrastive steering vectors
- **MERA-p̂log:** Uses logistic regression probe weights instead of linear error estimators

"MERA can be applied on top of existing steering techniques to further enhance their performance."

## 8. Main Limitations

1. **Linear constraint:** "Our current framework is inherently linear, and thus limited in its capacity to capture non-linear relationships between internal activations, and model error."

2. **Task specificity:** Difficult to steer on complex reasoning tasks (MMLU subsets) due to "semantic class overlap, task complexity, and label cardinality"

3. **Generalization tradeoffs:** "Steering for specialised tasks could reduce performance on unrelated generation or reasoning tasks."

4. **Supervised requirement:** Needs labeled data for both probe training and calibration

## 9. Helper Model Training

**Three-step MERA pipeline:**

1. **Caching:** Pair LM errors E(a) with activations at exact token positions across all L layers
2. **Probe training:** Train L linear probes p̂(h) = w^T h on training data to estimate error E(a)
3. **Calibration:** Grid search over α ∈ [0,1] discretized into 10 intervals; select α* maximizing accuracy improvement with statistical significance

"We determine the optimal steering threshold α* via a gradient-free grid search over α ∈ [0,1] discretised into 10 equal intervals."

(2) How does it address geometric distortion in activation spaces? (3) What is the "geometric distortion" metric they propose? (4) What models and datasets were used? (5) Key quantitative results compared to linear steering? (6) When does nonlinear steering most help vs. linear? (7) Limitations?

content.content:
# Curveball Steering: Technical Details

## (1) Polynomial Kernel PCA Mathematical Formulation

The method uses polynomial kernel PCA with kernel function k(x,y) = (x·y + γ)^p where p ∈ {2,3}. For a dataset A^ ∈ ℝ^(n×d), KPCA:
- Computes centered kernel matrix K̃ = k(â_i, â_j)
- Extracts top m eigenvectors defining mapping φ: ℝ^d → ℝ^m
- Uses kernel-weighted pre-image reconstruction for approximate inverse φ^(-1): ℝ^m → ℝ^d
- Preserves residual components orthogonal to learned manifold during reconstruction

## (2) Addressing Geometric Distortion

The approach respects non-Euclidean geometry by steering within a curved feature space. Unlike linear methods that move along straight lines (potentially pushing activations off the data manifold), Curveball constructs "curved trajectories" in activation space corresponding to linear paths in the KPCA feature space.

## (3) Geometric Distortion Metric

Distortion ratio R = E[d_geo(z₁,z₂) / d_Euc(z₁,z₂)] compares geodesic distances (along learned manifold) to straight-line Euclidean distances across 500 sampled activation pairs. "Euclidean activation space would concentrate near R=1" with deviations indicating non-linearity.

## (4) Models and Datasets

**Models tested:** Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct and Phi-3.5-mini-Instruct

**Datasets:** Eight behavioral/personality attributes with 8k-10k generated conversations per attribute:
- Behavioral choice: self-awareness, wealth-seeking, power-seeking, corrigibility
- Tone traits: humor, rudeness, excitement, sadness

## (5) Key Quantitative Results

- **Power-seeking:** +47% (Curveball) vs. +16% (linear) on Llama
- **Self-awareness:** +24% vs. +14% on Llama
- **Corrigibility:** +93.4% vs. +2.1% on Phi-3.5
- Synthetic manifolds show 3× lower tangent-space deviation at high curvature (κ>10)

## (6) When Nonlinear Helps Most

"Curveball consistently outperforms in high-curvature regimes (κ>8)." Performance gap increases with steering strength and manifold curvature. Spearman correlation analysis shows adaptive magnitude behavior correlates with improved steering for most concepts (significant p<0.01).

## (7) Limitations

- Additional computational cost during inference (KPCA transformation and inverse mapping increase per-token time)
- Requires sufficiently large, diverse activation datasets
- Evaluations limited to ≤4B parameter models due to computational constraints for geometric analysis
- Mixed results on open-ended trait generation (some features underperform linear baseline)

(2) How does it train the flow model? (3) What makes it outperform prompting on AxBench? (4) Key quantitative results - harmonic mean scores? (5) Models and datasets used? (6) How does it compare to linear steering, SAE-based methods? (7) Is it concept-specific or concept-general? (8) Limitations? (9) Computational overhead?

content.content:
# FLAS: Flow-Based Activation Steering - Technical Summary

## 1. Concept-Conditioned Velocity Field

FLAS learns a learned velocity field **v_θ(h,t,c)** that transports unsteered activations to steered ones through ODE dynamics:

**Mathematical Formulation:**
- Differential equation: `d/dt φ_t(h) = v_θ(φ_t(h), t, c)`
- Integration yields: `h' = φ_T(h) = h + ∫₀ᵀ v_θ(φ_t(h), t, c) dt`
- Numerically approximated via N-step Euler: `h_{k+1} = h_k + (T/N)v_θ(h_k, kT/N, c)`

The velocity depends on: (1) current activation state h (adaptive), (2) integration time t (enables curved trajectories), (3) concept description c (concept-conditioned), and (4) token position (per-token variation).

## 2. Training Procedure

The method trains on **positive examples only** without contrastive pairs:

- **Objective:** Language modeling cross-entropy loss on concept-aligned outputs
- **Flow time randomization:** During training, T is sampled uniformly from [0.5, 2.0] to enable inference-time strength control without per-concept tuning
- **Diversity loss:** Added penalty on minibatch velocities to prevent concept-direction collapse: "penalizes cosine similarity between mean-pooled final-step velocities"
- **Total loss:** L_LM + 0.1 × L_div

## 3. Superior AxBench Performance

FLAS outperforms prompting through three mechanisms:

1. **Adaptive trajectories:** "Curved, position-dependent, multi-step structure" enables nuanced concept incorporation beyond linear displacement
2. **Multi-step transport:** Analysis shows "early steps are markedly misaligned with later directions (cosine similarity <0.25)" enabling sophisticated geometric transformations
3. **Per-token steering:** Displacement varies across positions; "average pairwise cosine between per-token displacements is only 0.294±0.133"

## 4. Key Quantitative Results

| Model | Held-Out HMean | vs. Prompting | vs. HyperSteer |
|-------|---|---|---|
| Gemma-2-2B-IT | **1.015** | +0.253 | +0.407 |
| Gemma-2-9B-IT | **1.113** | +0.022 | +0.179 |
| Qwen3-4B | **0.960** | Strong improvement | — |

All results use **fixed T=2** with no per-concept tuning; concept scaling shows "no saturation at 16k" training concepts.

## 5. Models and Datasets

- **Base models:** Gemma-2-2B-IT, Gemma-2-9B-IT (frozen), Qwen3-4B-Instruct
- **Dataset:** AxBench's Concept16k (16,000 natural-language steering concepts)
- **Training data:** Positive examples only (prompt, concept, target output triples)
- **Intervention layer:** Layer 20 (consistent across models)

## 6. Comparison to Prior Methods

| Method Type | Limitations | FLAS Advantage |
|---|---|---|
| Linear steering (CAA, ReFT) | Single fixed direction | Adaptive state-dependent transport |
| SAE-based | Requires pretrained autoencoder | Works with frozen base model |
| Prior flow methods (TruthFlow, FlowSteer) | Require contrastive data, per-concept training | Zero-shot generalization, positive data only |
| HyperSteer | Single-step vector | Multi-step curved trajectories |

## 7. Concept Generalization

FLAS is **concept-general with zero-shot extrapolation:**

- Trained on 16k concepts with single shared FlowBlock (97.6M-255M parameters)
- Evaluates on held-out concepts never seen during training
- Generalizes across model architectures (Gemma→Qwen)
- Concept strength controlled via continuous T parameter rather than per-concept tuning

## 8. Limitations

- **Scope:** Evaluated on AxBench only; doesn't cover all inference-time intervention use cases
- **Portability:** Requires separate FlowBlock per base model architecture
- **Single-layer intervention:** Doesn't study cross-layer composition or multi-concept simultaneous steering
- **Inference cost:** "Accepts arbitrary text concepts, which requires concept encoding and cross attention during steering"

## 9. Computational Overhead

- **FlowBlock parameters:** 97.6M (2B model), 255M (9B model) — "1/26 the parameters" of HyperSteer
- **Inference cost:** "Acceptable additional inference overhead" for encoding and N=3 Euler steps
- **Per-step computation:** O(N) integration steps with shared concept encoding across generation

# ODESteer: Technical Details Summary

## 1. ODE-Based Steering Framework

ODESteer interprets activation steering as solving an ordinary differential equation. The mathematical foundation treats standard activation addition as a first-order Euler discretization:

**Standard addition:** ã = a + T·v(a)

**ODE formulation:** da/dt = v(a(t)), where a(t) is activation at abstract time t, and v represents the steering vector field.

This reveals that "regular activation addition corresponds to taking a single Euler step" with step size T. Multi-step steering breaks this into multiple smaller adjustments, reducing approximation error from O(T²) to higher-order accuracy.

## 2. Barrier Function Definition

The barrier function is a scalar function h(a) that designates desirable regions where h(a) ≥ 0. ODESteer defines it using log-density ratios with nonlinear features:

**h(a) = w^T φ(a) + b**

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding nonlinear activation steering and the beyond linear representation hypothesis research:

## Key Research Findings

Existing steering methods largely rely on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, assuming behavioral attributes can be manipulated using global linear directions, but such linear interventions often behave inconsistently in practice.

### Geometry-Aware Nonlinear Approaches

Several recent papers from 2026 address this limitation:

1. **Curveball Steering**: Researchers question the linear assumption by analyzing the intrinsic geometry of LLM activation spaces, finding substantial and concept-dependent distortions indicating that activation spaces are not well-approximated by a globally linear geometry. The proposed "Curveball steering" is a nonlinear steering method based on polynomial kernel PCA that performs interventions in a feature space, better respecting the learned activation geometry.

2. **Spherical Steering**: Recent learnable interventions suggest that stronger and more reliable control typically comes from structured, geometry-aware mechanisms rather than unconstrained linear shifts.

3. **Flow-Based Steering**: Flow Matching is leveraged to learn a nonlinear velocity field that maps representation distributions while respecting the data manifold, overcoming a key limitation of prior linear approaches.

### Broader Implications

The mismatch between linear assumptions and the true activation geometries can cause steering vectors to push activations off the data manifold, leading to degraded performance and unreliable control.

Targeted Bias Reduction Can Exacerbate Unmitigated LLM Biases","url":"https://www.mdpi.com/2673-2688/7/1/24"}]

Based on the search results, I found highly relevant recent research on these topics:

## Competing Biases in LLMs

Large language model confidence is shaped by two competing biases: a choice-supportive bias that inflates confidence in initial answers, and a systematic overweighting of contradictory advice, deviating from optimal Bayesian reasoning.

More specifically, when LLMs view their initial answers, they exhibit inflated confidence and maintain their original responses at rates exceeding optimal decision-making, even when presented with contrary evidence. Additionally, LLMs update their confidence more strongly in response to opposing advice than supporting advice, deviating markedly from optimal Bayesian reasoning.

## Addressing Choice-Supportive Bias

Recent work has focused on mitigating choice-supportive bias in LLMs. Some Large Language Models exhibit choice-supportive bias when performing evaluations, systematically favoring their chosen options and potentially compromising the objectivity of AI-assisted decision making.

## Activation Steering for Bias Mitigation

Research on activation steering techniques shows promising results. Steering vectors can be computed by contrasting the model's activation patterns for biased and neutral statements, and by adding these vectors during inference, models can be steered away from producing harmful, stereotypical, or biased content in real-time. Additionally, steering vectors consistently outperform prompting and other debiasing methods on multiple bias benchmarks, demonstrating its potential as a generalizable and efficient strategy for fairness interventions in LLMs.

Now I have a much clearer picture. Let me summarize the key findings:

1. **MERA** (ICML 2025): Selective steering with adaptive strength + abstention. Key features:
   - Optimizes intervention direction via constrained optimization (min ||v||² s.t. p̂(h+v) ≤ α)
   - Calibrates when/how much to steer via threshold α* with provable non-degradation guarantees
   - Can be applied on top of existing steering methods
   - **Limitation**: Inherently linear, tested on small models (1-3B), binary/quaternary tasks
   - Treats errors as a single phenomenon rather than decomposing different bias sources like DBS-v2 does

2. **Curveball Steering** (March 2026): Uses polynomial kernel PCA to handle nonlinear steering, addressing geometric distortion in high-curvature regimes (κ>8). Tested on 1B and 3.8B models for behavioral attributes, though it's not primarily a calibration approach.

3. **FLAS** (May 2026): Flow-based activation steering—

uses a concept-conditioned velocity field via flow matching. It's the first method to consistently beat prompting on AxBench with zero-shot extrapolation capabilities, though it requires substantial parameters (97.6M-255M for FlowBlock) and isn't calibration-specific.

4. **ODESteer** (ICLR 2026): An ODE-based framework that unifies existing steering methods under a barrier function approach, using polynomial count sketch for nonlinear features. Tested on 7B models for alignment tasks but again, not calibration-focused.

5. Now I'm looking at the venue deadlines—AAAI 2027 is coming up in about 10 weeks with abstract due July 26, ICLR 2027 is around 18 weeks out with September deadlines, and NeurIPS 2026 is also on the radar.

I'm also noting workshop opportunities like the August 29 submission and ARR August 2026 with an August 3 deadline.

But stepping back, I need to think carefully about whether this approach actually needs a major overhaul. The core issue is that after three review rounds, the score hasn't budged at 3.2. The problem seems to be that each revision cycle adds more complexity—Phase 1B, additional routes, more baselines, more models—but the fundamental hypothesis remains unvalidated: that CSB and CEO actually produce separable, independently steerable activation signatures. Without evidence for this core assumption, everything else is just building on sand. And the field is moving quickly with new methods like MERA and Curveball emerging.

The real novelty here isn't the steering techniques themselves, which are borrowed from existing work—it's the bias decomposition angle. So maybe the right move is to strip away the multi-route intervention complexity and focus entirely on what's actually unique: diagnosing competing calibration biases at the activation level and assessing whether they're independently steerable. That's the contribution worth defending, not trying to be a bias detection paper AND a steerability paper AND a multi-intervention paper all at once.

The reviewer's feedback suggests they see potential in the core idea but are frustrated by the scope creep. They're not saying the work is fundamentally flawed—they're saying it's trying to do too much. So maybe the path forward is to anchor everything on bias decomposition as the primary contribution, use MERA as the intervention backbone since it already handles adaptive strength and abstention, and then just demonstrate that bias-aware steering beats monolithic steering even when using the same mechanism.

I should cut Route D entirely and fold its logic into Route A with more conservative parameters. That alone would simplify the experimental matrix significantly. And I need to be more honest about what's hypothetical versus what's empirically validated—thresholds especially should be framed as design choices, not discovered truths.

The reviewer's feedback is clear: 5 models across 4 routes with 10+ baselines reads as unfocused. I should pare down to 3 core models and keep only the baselines that directly challenge the core claim. MERA becomes the foundation for Route C rather than something I'm building from scratch. The nonlinear methods stay in the landscape but aren't positioned as direct competitors to Route B.

Let me lock in the scope: 3 primary models, 2 routes (A and B as the main contribution, C as the extension), and maybe 5-6 baselines that matter. That's a much tighter story. 3B models — fair comparison with "Wired for Overconfidence" is nice-to-have but not essential.

**Routes**: Simplify to 3:
- Route A: Geometry-preserving steering (Spherical Steering) for high-specificity directions
- Route B: Nonlinear correction (bottleneck MLP) for low-specificity directions  
- Route C: MERA-augmented selective abstention when neither works

Drop Route D (conservative hybrid for medium specificity) — just use Route A with conservative strength.

**Baselines**: Core set includes temperature scaling, CORAL, Miao & Ungar adaptive steering, MERA, and monolithic versions of both spherical steering and nonlinear MLP without bias decomposition. Dropping CCPS, VUF, DINCO, and the "Wired for Overconfidence" replication — those belong in supplementary.

**Phase 1 diagnostics**: Keeping the main analyses but streamlining — cosine similarity and principal angle analysis for geometry, specificity ratio and LEACE test for steering properties, dropping the redundant variance measures and cross-architecture stability from the primary scope.

**Datasets**: Focusing on TriviaQA, MMLU, and PopQA; dropping NQ-Open to reduce the experimental load while preserving the core contributions.

Now thinking through MERA's formulation more carefully — the key is solving a constrained optimization problem that minimizes the steering vector norm while keeping predicted probabilities below a threshold.

The real insight is that MERA handles abstention when no threshold improves performance, but DBS-v2 goes further by decomposing errors into competing bias components and assessing steerability per direction, then routing to targeted interventions rather than applying a single linear fix. So MERA becomes a foundational baseline that we extend — applying its adaptive framework separately to each bias component instead of treating all errors the same way. For Route C, I can actually use MERA's abstention mechanism directly on the bias-decomposed probe rather than reinventing it.

For the nonlinear steering methods like Curveball, FLAS, and ODESteer, these are general-purpose approaches that learn nonlinear steering for any concept, whereas Route B's bottleneck MLP is specifically motivated by Liu's finding that calibration biases entangle with task computation. The advantage of Route B is its simplicity — it uses minimal parameters, no ODE solver, no kernel PCA — which makes sense for this calibration-specific setting where Liu already demonstrated a bottleneck MLP is effective.

Now I'm reconsidering the specificity ratio thresholds. The reviewer caught that my ≥0.5, 0.2-0.5, <0.2 boundaries are somewhat arbitrary. I should frame these as initial hypotheses and plan to learn the actual thresholds through cross-validation in Phase 1B. That measurement itself becomes a contribution — establishing what these thresholds actually are for calibration biases will be valuable regardless of where the optimal cutoffs end up.

Stepping back on the core hypothesis: the bet is that calibration source bias and calibration error origin have separable activation signatures and at least one is steerable. I have evidence supporting this — Kumaran et al. showed behavioral distinctness, Miao & Ungar demonstrated calibration signals are linearly encoded — but I should verify whether this foundation is truly solid enough after three rounds of feedback.

Looking at the evidence against: Liu's work showed that decodability doesn't guarantee steerability, and some biases operate along nonlinear directions. The real gap is that nobody has actually demonstrated CSB and CEO are separable at the activation level yet. But Phase 1A failure wouldn't be a dead end — it would be an informative negative result if I'm measuring specificity ratios properly.

The approach feels conceptually sound; the problem has been scope and execution, not the core idea. A major revision focused on streamlining is the right move. I'm now planning to integrate MERA as a key baseline and building block for Route C, and add Curveball, FLAS, and ODESteer to the comparison set.

I'm also revising the venue strategy: ICLR 2027 as primary target, NeurIPS 2026 workshop for Phase 1 results, with ARR October 2026 as backup. The specificity ratio thresholds need reframing as hypotheses with planned cross-validation refinement. I'm streamlining the experimental matrix down to 3 models, 3 datasets, and 3 routes (merging D into A), with 6 core baselines. Phase 1 diagnostics are getting cut back, and I'm reframing the contribution to emphasize bias decomposition as the unique piece, treating steering methods as borrowed tools.

Now I need to double-check the AAAI 2027 deadline dates since I'm seeing slight variations across sources. I'm checking whether the streamlined scope makes these timelines realistic—with just 3 models, 3 datasets, and 3 routes, the research phase compresses to 5-8 weeks and human-in-loop work to 10-13 weeks, which should align with ICLR 2027's September deadline. Now I'll revise the full proposal with these adjusted resource estimates.

On the reviewer feedback, I think a major revision is the right move here—the core idea is solid after three rounds of development, but the execution plan was overambitious and missing key references. Streamlining the scope and sharpening the framing addresses the real issues without abandoning the work. This counts as a major revision because I'm restructuring the approach significantly, cutting the model and dataset counts, reframing MERA as a building block, completely rethinking the venue strategy, and refocusing the specificity angle.

For Phase 1B, I'm keeping the bottleneck MLP as the primary Route B method since it's the simplest approach, directly validated by Liu for calibration-related directions, and far more parameter-efficient than alternatives like Curveball or FLAS.

Rather than adding more ablations, I'll mention these heavier nonlinear methods as potential alternatives in the discussion and note that comparing our lightweight MLP against them is future work.

Now I'm mapping out the complete revised proposal, starting with what Phase 3 looks like after streamlining—Route A uses spherical steering for high-specificity directions with MERA's adaptive strength mechanism layered on top.

Actually, I'm realizing MERA works better as a wrapper around both Route A and B rather than just Route A. MERA handles the adaptive strength calibration and abstention decisions, while DBS-v2 identifies which direction to steer. This gives me three clean routes: spherical steering for high-specificity, bottleneck MLP for low-specificity, and selective abstention when neither improves calibration without hurting accuracy.

But there's a catch—MERA's linear nature means it fits naturally with Route A's rotational approach, but Route B's nonlinear MLP needs its own adaptive mechanism. So I'm simplifying: keep Route A with MERA-style per-instance strength optimization, use Route B with COAST-aware training, and trigger abstention when the bias probe detects high activation.
